Béchamel (also spelled bechamel) is a smooth, creamy, white sauce used in cooking. It is one of the most important and widely used sauces in Western cuisine, particularly in French and Italian cooking.

Béchamel is a thick, silky sauce made from just three basic ingredients: butter, flour, and milk. That's it. The result is a pale, off-white sauce with a rich, creamy taste and a smooth, velvety texture.
How it is made (so you understand what it actually is)

To truly understand what béchamel is, it helps to know how it comes together:

  1. Butter is melted in a pan over gentle heat.
  2. Flour is stirred into the melted butter and cooked briefly. This mixture of butter and flour is called a roux (pronounced "roo"). The roux is what gives béchamel its thickness.
  3. Milk is added gradually — a little at a time — while stirring constantly. This prevents lumps from forming.
  4. The mixture is cooked over low heat, stirring continuously, until it thickens into a smooth, creamy sauce.
  5. It is seasoned with salt, white pepper, and often a small pinch of nutmeg, which gives it a subtle warmth.

The key thing to understand is that the roux (butter + flour) acts as a thickener. When milk is added to it and heated, the starch in the flour absorbs the liquid and causes the sauce to thicken. This is the science behind why béchamel has that characteristic thick, coating consistency.
What it looks like and tastes like

Béchamel is white to pale cream in color. It is glossy and smooth — not grainy, lumpy, or watery. It has a mild, milky, slightly buttery flavor with a gentle savory quality. It does not have a sharp or overpowering taste on its own; it is intentionally neutral so that it can blend well with other ingredients in a dish.

Its consistency can range from quite thin (almost like a thick cream) to quite thick (almost like a paste), depending on how much flour and butter are used relative to the milk.
Why it matters — its role in cooking

Béchamel is one of the five French "mother sauces" — a group of foundational sauces from which hundreds of other sauces are derived. Think of mother sauces as the building blocks of Western cooking. Once you have béchamel, you can create many other sauces simply by adding one or two more ingredients to it.

For example:

  • Add cheese (usually Gruyère or Parmesan) to béchamel → you get Mornay sauce, used in mac and cheese and cheese gratins.
  • Add puréed onions → you get Soubise sauce.
  • Add cream and crayfish butter → you get Nantua sauce, used in seafood dishes.
Where you encounter béchamel in real dishes

Béchamel is used in a remarkable range of everyday dishes around the world:

  • Lasagna: The creamy white layer between pasta sheets is béchamel.
  • Moussaka: The Greek dish has a thick layer of béchamel baked on top.
  • Croque Monsieur: The classic French grilled ham-and-cheese sandwich is spread with béchamel.
  • Gratins: Dishes like potato gratin or cauliflower gratin are coated in béchamel before being baked until golden and bubbling.
  • Soufflés: Béchamel forms the creamy base of many savory soufflés.
  • Mac and cheese: Most recipes use béchamel (with cheese stirred in) to create the creamy sauce that coats the pasta.
  • Croquettes: These fried snacks often have a thick béchamel filling inside.
  • Cannelloni and pasta bakes: Béchamel is poured over stuffed pasta tubes before baking.

What makes béchamel so universally beloved and useful is its versatility and neutrality. Because it has a mild flavor, it can be used in dishes ranging from subtle vegetable bakes to rich meat casseroles. It adds creaminess and body to a dish without competing with the main flavors. It also acts as a binder — it holds ingredients together in baked dishes and prevents them from drying out in the oven.

In everyday cooking language, if someone says a dish is "made with béchamel" or "has a béchamel sauce," you can picture a creamy, white, smooth, and rich coating or layer that brings richness and comfort to the dish.
